newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels strike new propaganda blow on poverty.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels strike new propaganda blow on poverty.

text.p: Marxist rebels launched a fresh propaganda offensive on Saturday unfurling banners at the Japanese ambassador's home that struck comparisons between their VIP hostages, Peru's poor and their jailed comrades.
"Most of the population would like to feed themselves as well as the authorities held here," read one message, referring to the meals provided daily by the Red Cross in the 32-day siege.

On two more banners the rebels said the captive officials were "responsible for the government's policies that affect the people" and that the guerrillas' jailed comrades also had families that wanted freedom for their relatives.
Local television showed three rebels in the early hours scurrying across the diplomatic mansion's roof, from where they they hung down large, white sheets with neat red letters.

About half an hour later, the men came out again to erect their red and white Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) flag that depicts a mace and rifle flanking a long-haired 18th century Indian revolutionary leader.

One of the rebels wore blue jeans, while the others were dressed in black combat gear. Apparently conscious of the television coverage, one of the men waved his arms in the air as he scuttled back inside the residence.

Since storming the fortified compound Dec. 17, the rebels have released more than 550 of the guests they originally seized at a lavish cocktail party. The remaining 73 hostages include top government and security force officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori.
They have held onto those they consider the best bargaining chips to force the government to give in to their main demand that some 400 jailed comrades are released.
Throughout the siege, the rebels have repeatedly showed signs carrying messages reiterating their political beliefs or responding directly to government statements on the crisis.

In their latest mesages, the guerrillas ignored the opportunity of replying to a government claim that the two sides -- apparently entrenched in uncompromising positions -- had edged closer on Friday by agreeing to a second round of face-to-face talks.
Official negotiator Domingo Palermo said the government was ready to resume talks with the rebels but would not accept their main demand of freedom for about 400 of rebels' imprisoned comrades.
Palermo told a news conference arrangements had been made for him to meet MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in a building near the besieged compound.

On Friday, the MRTA freed their first hostage release in 17 days. The rebels freed Luis Valencia Hirano, head of the Delta special forces unit of the anti-terrorist police DINCOTE, for health reasons.
Looking haggard and exhausted, Valencia still pumped his fist in the air as he left the building to applause from the hostages still inside.

"He was released so that he can resume his clinical treatment," said Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, accompanying Valencia. The Red Cross did not specify his medical condition but local media said he had heart problems.

The release was followed by a brief statement from Palermo that the government was ready to resume talks with the rebels but would not accept their main demand of freedom for about 400 of rebels' imprisoned comrades.
Canada's ambassador -- among the first hostages to be released by the rebels -- would sit on a "guarantor" peace commission overseeing the talks, he added.
Although Palermo presented the meeting as definite -- adding that a Red Cross vehicle would transport Cerpa to the site -- it was not clear if the MRTA had agreed to it.
The rebels broke off a previously planned meeting with Palermo over the government's refusal to discuss their main demand.
